episode.before: At parent 3d02d1da11ea4402f1a80c3df4df9fe57d53fe84, trust decisions applied only to the exact working directory; project instruction files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md triggered approval and were hidden when untrusted; interactive startup contained its own trust-resolution logic; package and config commands used separate, simpler rules and could not consult project_trust extensions or a configurable global default.
episode.after: At d041b5cc354f9361207708395033e87cc78576cd, passive project instruction files load regardless of trust, while approval is required only for project configuration or discovered skill directories. Trust decisions inherit from the nearest ancestor and may be persisted for a parent folder or limited to the session. A shared resolver applies explicit override, safe-input bypass, extension decision, persisted decision, global default, and fail-closed prompting in order. Interactive startup, package commands, and config commands use this resolver after a bootstrap pass that excludes project-local executable resources.
episode.diff: The change adds shared project-trust and startup-UI modules; extends the trust store with ancestor lookup, atomic multi-path updates, parent-folder choices, and saved-source reporting; narrows trust-input detection and ungates context-file loading; adds global ask/always/never policy; and routes normal startup plus package/config commands through the same trust-resolution pipeline. Tests cover inheritance and override clearing, passive instruction visibility, global-default precedence, extension-mediated package trust, and persisted-decision precedence.

evidence_units.claim: The pinned merge commit resolves PR #5549 as an implementation-bearing change titled "feat(ui): Improved project approval settings" with 26 coding-agent files changed.

Before the change, hasProjectTrustInputs treated AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md in the directory ancestry as approval-triggering inputs, and ProjectTrustStore.get read only the exact normalized working-directory key.
After the change, trust-input detection checks the current project's .pi directory and ancestral .agents/skills directories, but no longer treats AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md as trust-gated inputs.
Project context loading no longer accepts a projectTrusted flag and always collects context files from the working directory and its ancestors.
The resource-loader regression test proves that an untrusted project still exposes its AGENTS.md while extensions, skills, prompts, themes, and project settings remain excluded.

The trust store normalizes paths, walks toward the filesystem root to find the nearest explicit decision, reports the source path, and supports locked multi-path updates that can delete child overrides.
Trust choices now include trusting the current folder, trusting its parent while clearing the current override, session-only allow/deny choices, and persistent denial.
Trust-manager tests prove nearest-ancestor inheritance, child override precedence, and restoration of parent inheritance after atomically clearing the child override.
Trust-selector tests prove inherited-decision labeling and that selecting parent trust returns coordinated parent-save and child-clear updates.

The shared resolver orders trust policy as explicit override, automatic approval when no gated inputs exist, extension hook, persisted nearest-path decision, global ask/always/never default, and finally UI selection or fail-closed denial when no UI or selection is available.
The global settings manager exposes defaultProjectTrust with ask as the fallback for absent or invalid values and persists changes only in global settings.
Settings tests prove that project-local settings cannot override the global default trust policy and that invalid values resolve to ask.
The resource loader provides a bootstrap pass that forces untrusted settings before loading only the current safe extension set, then reloads full resources after trust resolution.

Package and config commands construct an initially untrusted settings manager, optionally load bootstrap trust extensions, invoke the shared resolver, set the resulting trust state, report warnings, and block local package mutations when untrusted.
Normal application startup invokes the shared resolver with the global default, bootstrap extensions, UI context, and extension-error reporting before resource loading continues.

Package-command tests prove that the global always policy enables project packages, project_trust extensions can approve package commands, and an explicit trust-store denial overrides the global always policy.
The parent implementation embedded trust resolution in main and used a separate package-command rule, while the new implementation extracts the resolver and routes both command paths through it.

title: Preserve dangerous-command detection across newline-separated command fragments
before: At parent commit 7b23dbfe6841002328f96e8d97980e1d11410db5, the dangerous-command detector evaluated each configured regular expression with re.IGNORECASE only. Patterns containing `.*`, including remote-content pipes, disk-copy commands, and recursive permission changes, therefore did not span newline characters; representative multiline forms returned non-dangerous and could avoid the approval boundary.
after: At commit 7166647ca132d54149af35dfd21312a1e3c19625, the detector evaluates every dangerous-command pattern with `re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL`, so wildcard portions span newline characters. Four regression cases establish that newline-separated curl-to-shell, wget-to-shell, disk-copy, and recursive chmod forms are classified as dangerous before the approval orchestrator decides whether execution requires approval.
diff: The implementation changes the shared regex invocation in `detect_dangerous_command` from `re.search(pattern, command_lower, re.IGNORECASE)` to `re.search(pattern, command_lower, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL)`. The test suite adds `TestMultilineBypass` with four multiline command examples. No patterns, approval-state rules, allowlists, prompting behavior, or isolated-environment exemptions are changed.

episode.title: Preserve dangerous-command detection across newline-separated command fragments
episode.before: At parent commit 7b23dbfe6841002328f96e8d97980e1d11410db5, the dangerous-command detector evaluated each configured regular expression with re.IGNORECASE only. Patterns containing `.*`, including remote-content pipes, disk-copy commands, and recursive permission changes, therefore did not span newline characters; representative multiline forms returned non-dangerous and could avoid the approval boundary.
episode.after: At commit 7166647ca132d54149af35dfd21312a1e3c19625, the detector evaluates every dangerous-command pattern with `re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL`, so wildcard portions span newline characters. Four regression cases establish that newline-separated curl-to-shell, wget-to-shell, disk-copy, and recursive chmod forms are classified as dangerous before the approval orchestrator decides whether execution requires approval.
episode.diff: The implementation changes the shared regex invocation in `detect_dangerous_command` from `re.search(pattern, command_lower, re.IGNORECASE)` to `re.search(pattern, command_lower, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL)`. The test suite adds `TestMultilineBypass` with four multiline command examples. No patterns, approval-state rules, allowlists, prompting behavior, or isolated-environment exemptions are changed.

evidence_units.claim: Commit 7166647ca132d54149af35dfd21312a1e3c19625 has parent 7b23dbfe6841002328f96e8d97980e1d11410db5 and changes only `tools/approval.py` and `tests/tools/test_approval.py`, with 25 insertions and one deletion.
evidence_units.source: Local git: `git show --stat --format=fuller 7166647ca132d54149af35dfd21312a1e3c19625`; issue-bundle linked PR #233 commit and changed-file records.

evidence_units.claim: In the parent implementation, `detect_dangerous_command` lowercases the supplied command and searches each dangerous pattern using `re.IGNORECASE` without a flag that makes dot match newlines.
The resolution adds `re.DOTALL` to the shared `re.search` flags and makes no other production-code change.

The pattern table includes wildcard-dependent rules for recursive chmod, disk copy, and piping curl or wget content to a shell; applying DOTALL at the common search site extends these existing rules across line boundaries without duplicating or rewriting them.

`check_dangerous_command` is the approval orchestration entry point and calls `detect_dangerous_command(command)` before approval-state checks, prompting, or returning an approval-required response; therefore the matcher result controls entry into the approval path.

The added `TestMultilineBypass` class asserts dangerous classification for four commands whose relevant pattern fragments are separated by a backslash-newline: curl piped to sh, wget piped to bash, dd with `if=`, and recursive chmod followed by mode 777.
Directly evaluating the parent detector against the four added multiline examples produced `[False, False, False, False]`, confirming the pre-change bypass.
evidence_units.source: Local checkout command: streamed `git show 7b23dbfe6841002328f96e8d97980e1d11410db5:tools/approval.py` into Python 3 and invoked `detect_dangerous_command` for the four regression inputs.

evidence_units.claim: Directly evaluating the pinned implementation against the same four multiline examples produced `[True, True, True, True]`, confirming the post-change invariant for the represented pattern families.
evidence_units.source: Local checkout command: streamed `git show 7166647ca132d54149af35dfd21312a1e3c19625:tools/approval.py` into Python 3 and invoked `detect_dangerous_command` for the four regression inputs.

evidence_units.claim: Existing tests retain safe-command and recursive-delete checks, providing nearby regression coverage that the change does not intentionally redefine the pattern set or ordinary single-line classifications.

title: Broaden approved-command writes without weakening explicit filesystem denials
before: At parent de9e78e3e7caed0fdd75d20ae617faa646dfef3c, there was no executor-context operation that safely derived an approved-command filesystem policy by widening writes while retaining explicit path and glob read denials. Linux bubblewrap consumed separately resolved writable and unreadable roots; a writable bind of `/` could shadow the previously created minimal `/dev`, separate writable root-metadata mounts could follow symlinks and reopen denied targets, and deny-root resolution retained only effective targets rather than the literal paths needed to detect writable-symlink crossings. The execution capability contract also had no flags distinguishing support for these Linux behaviors.
after: At 645b683a9e712ae6d90a364e3cf597466e4146d0, restricted policies can be transformed for approved commands into root-wide and permitted root-metadata writes while preserving explicit path and glob denials. Transformation fails closed by returning the original policy when workspace-root denials cannot be materialized, the filesystem root cannot be determined, a deny matcher cannot be built, or the root itself is denied. Linux mount preparation inherits root-metadata access from a writable root, preserves literal deny paths, skips redundant aliases of `/`, recreates standard devices after binding `/`, and applies deny masks afterward. Executors advertise the two Linux guarantees through backward-compatible opt-in capability fields.
diff: The commit adds `FileSystemSandboxPolicy::for_approved_command`; adds Linux-specific writable-root and unreadable-root projections that prevent metadata remount and symlink-denial bypasses; changes bubblewrap mount construction to use those projections, avoid duplicate root-alias binds, and restore `/dev` after a writable root bind; adds two default-false, omitted-when-false capability fields; and adds policy, Windows volume, bubblewrap argument-order, standard-device, and root-metadata symlink regression tests. The commit changes 9 files with 780 insertions and 12 deletions.

commit.subject: Preserve filesystem denials when preparing approved commands (#48155)
commit.body_excerpt:
## Why

Approved commands need broader write access while retaining explicit read denials. On Linux, binding the filesystem root writable can shadow standard devices, and additional root-metadata mounts can reopen denied symlink targets.

## What changed

- Add `FileSystemSandboxPolicy::for_approved_command` to grant root and root-metadata writes while retaining path and glob denials. Keep the original policy when denials cannot be resolved or deny the root.
- Restore standard devices after Linux writable root binds, then apply explicit deny masks. Avoid redundant root-alias binds and inherit root-metadata writes from the root mount so denied targets stay masked.
- Preserve literal deny paths alongside resolved targets so Linux can reject denials that cross writable symlinks.
- Advertise L

The execution capability contract also had no flags distinguishing support for these Linux behaviors.
episode.after: At 645b683a9e712ae6d90a364e3cf597466e4146d0, restricted policies can be transformed for approved commands into root-wide and permitted root-metadata writes while preserving explicit path and glob denials. Transformation fails closed by returning the original policy when workspace-root denials cannot be materialized, the filesystem root cannot be determined, a deny matcher cannot be built, or the root itself is denied. Linux mount preparation inherits root-metadata access from a writable root, preserves literal deny paths, skips redundant aliases of `/`, recreates standard devices after binding `/`, and applies deny masks afterward. Executors advertise the two Linux guarantees through backward-compatible opt-in capability fields.
episode.diff: The commit adds `FileSystemSandboxPolicy::for_approved_command`; adds Linux-specific writable-root and unreadable-root projections that prevent metadata remount and symlink-denial bypasses; changes bubblewrap mount construction to use those projections, avoid duplicate root-alias binds, and restore `/dev` after a writable root bind; adds two default-false, omitted-when-false capability fields; and adds policy, Windows volume, bubblewrap argument-order, standard-device, and root-metadata symlink regression tests. The commit changes 9 files with 780 insertions and 12 deletions.

evidence_units.claim: Commit 645b683a states that approved commands require broader write access while retaining explicit read denials, and identifies Linux root binds shadowing devices and metadata mounts reopening denied symlink targets as the failures being corrected.
The pinned commit changes nine files, adding 780 lines and removing 12, including policy transformation, Linux mount construction, capability protocol, and regression tests.

`for_approved_command` starts from a restricted root-write policy, copies deny-read restrictions, materializes project-root references, validates a strict deny matcher, grants protected root-metadata writes only where not denied, and returns the original policy whenever safe materialization or root validation fails.

The policy layer adds a writable-root projection that suppresses separate protected-metadata mounts when `/` is writable, and an unreadable-root projection that retains literal deny paths alongside resolved targets for restricted policies.

Linux bubblewrap construction switches to the new writable and unreadable projections, detects a writable `/` bind, skips aliases resolving back to `/`, recreates the minimal `/dev` and `/dev/shm` after the root bind, and then applies explicit masks.

Policy tests cover Unix, Windows-drive, and UNC contexts; prove that root and allowed metadata become writable while explicit path and glob denials remain effective; and prove that root-denying or unresolvable denials leave the original policy unchanged.

The Windows sandbox policy test proves volume-root expansion grants writes on discovered volumes without restoring prior read/write grants, while retained denials and explicitly denied root metadata remain denied.

The managed-proxy Linux integration test runs an approved policy that can use `/dev/null`, `/dev/zero`, and `/dev/urandom` and write an output file, while reading the explicitly denied secret still fails with permission denied.

The root-metadata integration test proves metadata symlinks cannot reopen a denied directory, allowed metadata remains writable, writable-symlink crossings are rejected, and an explicit nested writable carveout reopens only that nested area.

The execution protocol adds two default-false capability flags for preserving devices under Linux root writes and preserving restrictions under approved root writes; false values are omitted from serialization and local Linux executors advertise both.
Protocol tests prove legacy capability payloads deserialize with both new flags false, false flags are absent on the wire, and independently enabled or fully enabled payloads round-trip.

The parent version lacks `for_approved_command`, the root-metadata inheritance mode, literal-path-preserving unreadable roots, root-bind device restoration, root-alias suppression, and the two capability fields.

candidate_workflows.description: Broaden an approved command's write effects only after retaining its negative access constraints, then realize the policy with platform-safe mount semantics and advertise the resulting guarantees explicitly.

workflow_graph.goal: Run an approved command with broad write access while preserving explicit read-denial boundaries and required runtime devices.
workflow_graph.entry_state: A command has been approved for broader writes, but its restricted policy includes explicit denials and the target executor may realize root-wide access through platform mounts or volume expansion.
workflow_graph.exit_state: The approved policy broadens writes without weakening retained denials; Linux realizes it without device loss, alias duplication, or metadata-symlink reopening; and consumers can detect support through backward-compatible capabilities.

call_sites: Linux bubblewrap construction switches to the new writable and unreadable projections, detects a writable `/` bind, skips aliases resolving back to `/`, recreates the minimal `/dev` and `/dev/shm` after the root bind, and then applies explicit masks.
tests: Policy tests cover Unix, Windows-drive, and UNC contexts; prove that root and allowed metadata become writable while explicit path and glob denials remain effective; and prove that root-denying or unresolvable denials leave the original policy unchanged.

The Windows sandbox policy test proves volume-root expansion grants writes on discovered volumes without restoring prior read/write grants, while retained denials and explicitly denied root metadata remain denied.

The managed-proxy Linux integration test runs an approved policy that can use `/dev/null`, `/dev/zero`, and `/dev/urandom` and write an output file, while reading the explicitly denied secret still fails with permission denied.

The root-metadata integration test proves metadata symlinks cannot reopen a denied directory, allowed metadata remains writable, writable-symlink crossings are rejected, and an explicit nested writable carveout reopens only that nested area.
Protocol tests prove legacy capability payloads deserialize with both new flags false, false flags are absent on the wire, and independently enabled or fully enabled payloads round-trip.
